title: the exit door
hook: a boy at Death's door turns down every treasure for one question

segments.voice: Yesterday, maya, and the snake that was a rope. Your line was hold it lightly. Did you catch a snake on the path? Today, the word for where this whole path is headed. Day nineteen.

A boy named Nachiketa is sitting at the door of Death's house. In the Katha Upanishad, his father, in a burst of temper, has said: I give you to Death. So the boy goes. Yama, the lord of death, is away, and Nachiketa waits on the doorstep without food for three nights. When Yama comes home, he's embarrassed to have kept a guest waiting, and he offers the boy three wishes. The first two are easy. The third is a question: what happens to a person after death? Yama tries to talk him out of it. Ask for something else, he says. Ask for long life, sons and grandsons, cattle, gold, a kingdom. Nachiketa says no.
screen: `A BOY AT DEATH'S DOOR.` → `THREE WISHES.` → `TAKE THE GOLD INSTEAD.` → `NO.`

segments.voice: Nachiketa's answer is the heart of today's word. He tells Death that all those treasures wear out, that wealth will never satisfy a person, that even a long life is short. Keep your horses, he says. I want to know. And Yama, impressed, begins to teach him. That turn, from the list of things to the thing under the list, points straight at today's word. Moksha means release. Liberation. Freedom. The tradition speaks of the soul moving through birth after birth, bound by its own actions and desires, and moksha is the knot finally coming untied. Hindu thought names several aims of a good life: dharma, doing what's yours to do; artha, making a living; kama, love and pleasure. None of those are bad. Moksha sits beyond them, as the freedom the others point toward. What that freedom is, the schools describe differently. Advaita Vedanta says it's waking up to what day ten and day eleven already hinted: that atman, the self, is Brahman, and always was. Devotional schools, such as those centered on Krishna, describe it as living forever in the loving presence of God, never dissolved, never alone. Some schools teach that a person can be free before death, liberated while still living. Notice the shape of Nachiketa's choice. He doesn't hate gold. He just won't trade the real question for it. That's the word in an ordinary day too: the moment you see that the next thing on the list was never going to be enough.
screen: `KEEP YOUR HORSES. I WANT TO KNOW.` · `MOKSHA — RELEASE. THE KNOT UNTIED.` · `BEYOND DUTY, WEALTH AND PLEASURE.` · `ATMAN IS BRAHMAN, OR LOVE WITH GOD.` · then, large: `FREEDOM IS THE POINT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set one thing down. Sit and breathe. Notice one thing you want right now. A message back, a better week, a number on a screen. Let the wanting be there. Now, just for the length of this sit, set it down beside you. Not forever. Just: for now, I don't need it. Breathe, and notice what's left when the wanting rests. If you pray, you can hold that space open to God. The bell holds the time.
Moksha. Release. Liberation. The knot untied, the freedom the other aims of life point toward. Nineteenth word.
Your line: freedom is the point. Once today, when you catch yourself chasing the next thing, set it down for one breath, the way Nachiketa set down the gold. Day nineteen.

howItsDone: In Hindu thought moksha is named alongside dharma, artha and kama as an aim of life, and seekers pursue it through knowledge, devotion, selfless action and meditation, with each school describing liberation in its own way.

fork.setup: you're Nachiketa. Death offers you long life, gold, cattle and a kingdom if you'll drop your question about what happens after death. what do you do?
options: take the kingdom. a long life is a good life.
take the gold and ask the question later.
turn it all down and keep the question.
fork.reveal: he turns it all down: the treasures wear out and wealth never satisfies. Yama, impressed, starts to teach him.

what a scholar hears: the purusharthas, dharma, artha, kama, moksha; and Katha Upanishad 1.1, where Nachiketa refuses Yama's gifts for the question of death.

sources.ref: Katha Upanishad 1.1 (Nachiketa and Yama, the three boons)

notes: Katha Upanishad: three nights without food, three boons, and Yama's offers (long life, sons and grandsons, cattle, gold, horses, a kingdom) paraphrased from 1.1; 'keep your horses' and 'wealth will never satisfy a person' paraphrase 1.1.26–27. Max Müller 1884 (SBE 15) translates this; not quoted because exact wording unverified. Confirm verse numbers.
The three boons: the script calls the first two 'easy' (his father's peace and the fire ritual); confirm the simplification.
Purusharthas named without stating a count; confirm the one-line glosses (dharma, artha, kama).
Moksha described two ways without ranking: Advaita (atman is Brahman) and devotional Vaishnava schools (eternal loving presence of God). Jivanmukti given as 'some teachers say'. Confirm.
Reference back to days 10 and 11 (atman, Brahman) matches the camp-one word list.
Nachiketa returns at length in the Katha Upanishad reading (y1 days 245 onward); day 19 only introduces the refusal of the gifts. Check for overlap.

Editor pass: 'that turn is moksha' softened to 'points straight at today's word' (the Katha passage doesn't use the word moksha); 'devotional schools, like those who worship Krishna' reworded; the myth item 'the schools all describe moksha the same way' replaced, since days 10, 11 and 18 already used that pattern.

Audit (2026-10-01): Katha 1.1 details checked (father's 'to Death I give you', three nights unfed, three boons, Yama's offers, 1.1.26-27 refusal); no errors. 'Some teachers say a person can taste it before death' undersold jivanmukti, which Advaita teaches as full liberation while living; now 'some schools teach that a person can be free before death'. The third boon is strictly the doubt whether a person exists after death; 'what happens after death' kept as a plain-language gloss.
